theme: The humble king on a donkey; the shepherd-king
readingInstruction: Read Zechariah 9:1-11:17. A king comes to Zion on a donkey, and a shepherd is rejected and sold for thirty pieces of silver. These chapters are rich in messianic promises, and the New Testament quotes them often. Read 9:9-10 and 11:12-13 slowly.
settingTheScene: The second half of Zechariah is made of two oracles, chapters 9 to 11 and 12 to 14. They are set in a different style than the visions, and they look to the distant future. They describe the coming of the king, the rejection of the shepherd, and the victory of the LORD. This reading covers the first oracle. The memory verse of this unit comes from chapter 9.
observation: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem!” (9:9).
“Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey” (9:9).
“I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem” (9:10).
“And he shall speak peace to the nations; his rule shall be from sea to sea” (9:10).
“As for you also, because of the blood of my covenant with you, I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit” (9:11).
“Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope” (9:12).
“Then I took my staff Grace, and I cut it in two, annulling the covenant that I had made with all the peoples” (11:10).
“So they weighed out as my wages thirty pieces of silver” (11:12).
interpretation:
Chapter 9 begins with judgment on the nations around Israel, Syria, Tyre, and Philistia, as God clears the way for his people. Then the focus narrows to a single, striking image: a king arrives in Jerusalem. Everything about him is surprising. He is “righteous and having salvation.” He is “humble,” or “afflicted.” And he rides a donkey, not a war horse. The donkey was a sign of peace and humility. Kings rode horses to war; they rode donkeys when they came in peace (1 Kings 1:33).

His kingdom is likewise surprising. He cuts off the chariot and war horse and the battle bow, and “speaks peace to the nations.” His rule reaches from sea to sea. This is a king of peace whose reign is universal, and whose weapon is speech. The Hebrew reading is that his word does it.

Then, “because of the blood of my covenant with you,” the prisoners are set free. Notice the phrase “prisoners of hope.” Even those who are still in the pit have hope, for a ransom is coming. The covenant is sealed in blood.

Chapters 10 and 11 shift. The people have followed false shepherds. God will care for his flock. But in chapter 11, Zechariah is told to play the part of a shepherd and to care for a doomed flock. He takes two staffs, “Favor” and “Union.” The flock rejects him, and he asks for his wages. They weigh out thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32). The LORD says, “Throw it to the potter,” and Zechariah throws the silver into the house of the LORD. It is a bitter irony: the shepherd is valued at the price of a slave.

The final verses describe the worthless shepherd who abandons the flock. This section of Zechariah shows two kings: the humble king who comes in peace and the shepherd who is rejected. They are one person.
connection: Matthew 21:1-11 shows Jesus entering Jerusalem on a donkey, quoting Zechariah 9:9. Matthew 26:15 records Judas receiving thirty pieces of silver. Matthew 27:3-10 records the silver being thrown into the temple and used to buy the potter’s field. Luke 22:20: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.” John 10:11: “I am the good shepherd.” Philippians 2:5-8 describes Christ’s humility.
application:
Read Matthew 21:1-11 alongside today’s reading. Notice how precisely Jesus fulfilled Zechariah.

Think about humility in your leadership or relationships. What does it look like to come in peace, “on a donkey”?

Thank Jesus for being the shepherd who was sold for thirty pieces of silver for you.
prayerPrompts: Rejoice that your King has come, humble and riding on a donkey.
Tell him what you want to say to the shepherd-king.
